messages.subject: [statnet_help] Helpful info on the degeneracy warning in the ergm output
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Helpful info on the degeneracy warning in the ergm output
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Many of you may have noticed a warning about possible degeneracy that 
appears at the end of many calls to the function "ergm" in the latest 
version of statnet. After a number of questions on the topic, and some of 
our own research into the matter, we've determined that this diagnostic 
can be rather liberal in its diagnosis of degeneracy.  That is, it often 
suggests that degeneracy is present, when it actually is not.

Our advice is to treat the warning as it was intended to be - a 
suggestion, not a definitive diagnosis.  We strongly advise that users 
check all of their models that are fit through MCMC by using the much more 
extensive built-in MCMC diagnostics. These can be accessed using the 
function mcmc.diagnostics(). Note that this command generates two plots 
for each statistic in your model, so it is generally wise to send the 
output to an external file.  For example:

pdf("my.diagnostic.plots.pdf")
mcmc.diagnostics(my.ergm.fit)
dev.off()

You can see examples of these plots and advice on how to interpret them in 
the JSS statnet tutorial:

http://www.jstatsoft.org/v24/i09

and read more about degeneracy diagnostics in the JSS ergm paper:

http://www.jstatsoft.org/v24/i03

In future versions of ergm, we will be turning off the warning as a 
default, and perhaps making changes to its parameters.  In the meanwhile, 
those users who wish to turn it off can add the following argument to 
any of their calls to the ergm function:

control.ergm(check.degeneracy=FALSE)

Happy fitting!
Steve
On behalf of the Statnet team

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Options for testing for triad closure effects
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Options for testing for triad closure effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi Statnet-ers!
What are your preferred methods for testing for triad closure effects in
your erg models of graphs & digraphs, and do you have an implicit
(or even explicit) decision tree to decide among the options?

Some of the apparently relevant ergm-terms include:
* ctriad, ttriad (directed only)
* dsp, esp
* gwdsp, gwesp
* localtriangle
* triangle (usually with a "star" variant)
* tripercent

I read David's 2007 "Curved Exponential Family Models for Social Networks"
article as suggesting that the geometrically weighted methods may be 
superior
to the kstar(2)+triangle construction, but was left with a number of 
questions:
* if using a geometrically weighted term, must all the terms (gwdegree, 
gwdsp,
   gwesp)be used together, or which subsets are sufficient for triad 
closure?
* how does one choose appropriate alphas for gwdsp & gwesp (in the article,
   the alphas appeared to be 1 or 0 only).
 
Thanks!
Brian

--

messages.body_plain:
I've been experimenting with importing pajek data using the read.paj  
routine in the network package; it appears to only import the vertex  
names as attributes, while ignoring the other verted attributes. For  
example, in the read.paj documentation, one of the examples is:

test.net.1 <- read.paj("http://vlado.fmf.uni-lj.si/pub/networks/data/GD/gd98/A98.net 
")

However, the object imported only has vertex.names attribute, ignoring  
the other three columns of data attached to each vertex in the file,  
e.g. vertex 1 in the file is:

      1 "www.att.com/catalog/consumer"           0.2512    0.4239     
0.5000

But in R, only the names are brought in:

 > list.vertex.attributes(test.net.1)
[1] "na"           "vertex.names"

 > get.vertex.attribute(test.net.1,"vertex.names")[1]
[1] "www.att.com/catalog/consumer"

Are there plans to expand the import function? I'm not familiar enough  
with the package to contribute a patch at the moment.

Thanks
-AHM

messages.subject: [statnet_help] actor specific random effects
messages.body_plain:
Hello dear all,

I want to estimate a logit model of link formation in the random  
effects tradition. I assume that when actor-specific effects (e.g. a_i  
is effect for actor i) are given, link formation becomes independent  
from the rest of the network. The actor-specific effects are assumed  
to be uncorrelated with covariates. The LOGIT MODEL can be written as:

Prob(y_ij = 1|x_ij,beta,a_i,a_j) = exp(x_ij' %*% beta + a_i + a_j)/ (1  
+ exp(x_ij' %*% beta + a_i + a_j))

, where y_ij = y_ji = 1 if i has link with j, x_ij dyad covariates,  
beta are coefficients and the actor specific effects a_i are  
distributed iid Normal(0,sig^2).

The usual way is to integrate out the a's for estimation. This case is  
special because integration needs to be done over the whole quality  
function not only the contribution of one observation (one firm-pair).

As OPTIMIZATION EXAMPLE take MLE, where the likelihood of one network would be

L(Y | X,beta,a_1,...,a_n) = Product_(i=1)_(n-1) ( Product_(j=i+1)_(n)  
( Prob(y_ij = 1|x_ij,beta,a_i,a_j)))

and optimization should be done for L(Y | X,beta,sig_a), which is an  
integral of L(Y | X,beta,a_1,...,a_n) with respect to a_1..a_n.

THE PROBLEM is that neither in the statnet package nor any other  
package I found an appropriate function to estimate the model.

1. Is anybody aware of such a function????
2. If not, which algorithms would you suggest to solve the problem?  
(B.t.w. the network consists of 240 nodes.)

Thank you very much
Moritz Mueller

messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet_help,

I've coded a new user term into the most recent ergm package source  
code, which I call "wagonwheels".  The most basic wagonwheel is  
equivalent to a triangle and I've been able to obtain the same counts  
on a given network from:

 > summary(nw ~ wagonwheel(1))

as

 > summary(nw ~ triangle)

Using 'summary' for more complex wagonwheels also obtains correct  
counts for my own toy examples.

However, when I attempt to fit a model with ergm(nw ~ wagonwheels(1)),  
things go horribly awry!  Specifically, "all the MCMC sample  
statistics are the same"; as a result, the wagonwheels1 estimate is  
stuck on the initial value.

Does anyone have any ideas as to what might be going wrong?

Thanks in advance,
- Art.

It replaces the lines in read.paj that usually just read in the vertex

I don't know if there's a test suite of .net or .paj files against  
which to check these...  the code currently makes some assumptions  
about the first three attributes being coordinates...

            if (nrow(as.data.frame(vertex)) == network.size(temp)) {
                temp <- set.vertex.attribute(temp, "vertex.names",
                  as.character(vertex[as.numeric(vertex[,1]),2]))
                if (ncol(vertex)>2) { # number of columns > 2 ->  
vertex has attributes
                  vert.attr.nam <- c("na","vertex.names","x","y","z")  
#assume first three are coords (true?)
                  if (ncol(vertex)>5) vert.attr.nam <- c(vert.attr.nam, 
6:ncol(vertex)) #temp names for rest
                  for (vert.attr.i in 3:ncol(vertex)){
                    v <- vertex[,vert.attr.i]
                    if (is.factor(v)){ # if it's a factor, then
                      vert.attr.nam.tmp <- levels(v)[1] # see if the  
first factor is an attribute name
                      if (vert.attr.nam.tmp=="") vert.attr.nam.tmp <-  
levels(v)[2] # in case of missing data
                      if (nlevels(v)<=2&! 
is.na(match(vert.attr.nam.tmp, # check for match if # factors <=2
                                    
c("s_size","x_fact","y_fact","phi","r","q",
                                     "ic","bc","bw","lc","la","lr",
                                     "lphi","fos","font")))) { #from  
pajekman.pdf v1.2.3 p.69-70
                        vert.attr.nam[vert.attr.i+1] <-  
vert.attr.nam.tmp #if match, name the next column
                      } else { #if not, set the attribute, converting  
to character (networks incompat w/factors)
                        temp <-  
set.vertex.attribute(temp,vert.attr.nam[vert.attr.i],
                                                      
as.character(vertex[as.numeric(vertex[,1]),vert.attr.i]))
                      }
                    } else { #not a factor, set the attribute and  
don't convert to character
                      temp <-  
set.vertex.attribute(temp,vert.attr.nam[vert.attr.i],
                                                    
vertex[as.numeric(vertex[,1]),vert.attr.i])
                    }
                  }
                }
               if (debug)
                  print("set vertex names to matrix")
            }

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Options for testing for triad closure effects
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Options for testing for triad closure effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

My own experience is that triangle, tripercent, ctriad and ttriad are 
often degenerate for all but the smallest networks.  Still, they're the 
simplest to interpret, so it might be worth giving them a try on your 
network just to see.  But I myself end up using gwesp pretty much all the 
time now. I've never used localtriangle, but that doesn't mean it wouldn't 
be useful to others!

In terms of gwesp, gwdsp, gwd as a group vs. individual; I guess this 
depends partly on what you're trying to model, and your philosophical 
bent.  If you are coming at your model via a belief that your network 
exhibits the "realization dependent" one-step-out-from-Markov dependence 
discussed in Snijders et al. ("New specifications...") then you should 
probably include all three.  But, I personally tend to focus more on GWESP 
when I'm specifically interested in triangle effects, since that's the one 
that relates most obviously to them for me. I think GWD's interpretation 
is more related to degrees (hence the name), whereas GWDSP is a bit harder 
to pin down (at least for me.)  It gives one a sense of the tendency for 
any two actors tend to have the same friends in common, regardless of 
whether they are connected or not; whereas GWESP does this only for actors 
who are themselves tied.  So I like to think of GWDSP as providing a kind 
of global measure of structural equivalence (in the sense that it captures 
the process whereby if two actors have a common partner, they're now more 
likely than otherwise to have their additional partners in common.)

In some sense (now that I'm on a roll with pondering this issue), 
including both GWDSP and GWESP allows for the resulting coefficient of 
GWESP to be more clearly interpretable as a triangle effect than when one 
includes only GWESP.  That's because there are two different phenomena 
being measured in GWESP (the tendency for triangles to close, and the 
tendency for those with partners in common to have various counts of them) 
whereas GWDSP only includes the latter of these two. including both terms 
means GWDSP can model the latter process, and GWESP is free to capture the 
former process more cleanly.  Now I'm only brainstorming, I've not thought 
about this deeply.  In some sense it may be a largely academic question, 
since in every large network I've tried fitting GWDSP to (ie the Add 
Health schools), its coefficient is very close to 0 and not at all 
significant, with or without GWESP in the model as well. You might try it 
as well and see; I'd be interested to see if you get the same thing.

Yours,
Steve

and move high.  This works whether you're using FIXED=F in these terms and 
allowing the algorithm to find the most likely value of alpha for you, or 
finding a good value yourself using multiple runs and comapring them by 
some means.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Art,

A quick check- in one place in the code below you have the term as 
"wagonwheel", and in the other as "wagonwheels."  I'm guessing this is 
just a typo in the email, and doesn't actually have anything to do with 
causing the problem.  Assuming that's right, then the first thing I would 
suggest doing is fitting the same ergm model with triangle instead of 
wagonwheels(1) -- that is, do:

ergm(nw ~ wagonwheels(1))

to see if you get the same problem.  That will help clarify whether there 
is a reason why wagonwheel(1)/triangle doesn't work well for your dataset 
(i.e. it's a degenerate model, perhaps), or whether there's sonething in 
wagonwheel(1) that needs debugging.  You can respond to me individually, 
if you wish.

Steve
